title: A timestamp a client sends carries its UTC offset
intent: A date and time without a UTC offset names no instant: ten in the morning is a different moment in every zone. Stored as if it were UTC, it puts a writer in any other zone off by that zone's offset, and nothing reports it. The published API contract already asks for the offset, since a date-time there is the RFC 3339 form, whose offset is required. So timestamp text without one is refused wherever a request schema reads it, and a declared filter refuses a bound without one; the refusal names the fix. Reading a value without an offset as UTC, for a sender known to send UTC without saying so, is the framework's one way around it, and it is an escape a person decides and a reviewer sees.
reference: The rule fails closed by name. Every reference to NaiveMeansUtc is refused: as a name, as an attribute (core.NaiveMeansUtc, terp.core.NaiveMeansUtc), through getattr with that literal name, and in a quoted annotation. So is every name the file binds to it by an import alias, an assignment or a type alias, at each use where that binding is the one in scope, and a class attribute bound to it at each use through its class. A class or a re-export of that name from anywhere counts too, and so does reaching terp.core.timestamps, the boundary's own module, however it is spelled (an import of it, from terp.core import timestamps, an attribute of the terp.core package or a getattr of it by that literal name, and its dotted name written as a literal, as importlib and sys.modules are handed it); an attribute called timestamps on anything else is the app's own. A Literal value is text, not the escape. A plain datetime field needs nothing, and neither does a datetime query parameter forwarded to a declared filter: at run time BaseSchema refuses timestamp text without an offset wherever Pydantic reads a datetime for it, as a 422 at its place, and the filter refuses a bound without one as a 400 that names it (ADR 0206). The rule holds every root that ships Python, a worker as much as the app; terp.core, which defines the boundary and its escape, is neither's user.

runtime.rationale: The schema holds the invariant itself. BaseSchema puts the refusal in front of every datetime Pydantic validates for it, following every definition the schema refers to: in a field, a list, a mapping, a union, a type alias, a dataclass, a TypedDict or a nested BaseSchema, under the name Pydantic reads it by, so timestamp text without a UTC offset is a 422 at its place; a declared filter refuses a bound without one as a 400 that names the filter. A nested model that brings its own complete validator, which does not judge, has what it is given judged first, under its own config, before that validator reads it unchanged; a subclass that defines either hook the base relies on is refused when it is defined. The marks the refusal trusts are objects compared by identity, in a module the build-time half refuses to an app. The build-time half governs the framework's one way around the refusal, so taking it is never quiet.
